 What is the best laptop you can buy in 2026? Choosing a laptop is no longer simply a question of MacBook versus Windows. The right pick depends on whether you need all-day portability for work or study, serious gaming and creative performance, a repairable machine you can upgrade, or an affordable device for everyday browsing and streaming.
 At Tom's Guide, we’ve tested the leading options across those needs to help you find the best fit. The MacBook Air M5 remains our top all-round choice, with its powerful everyday performance, lightweight design and excellent battery life for the price. But there are other options if you want a Windows machine, a dedicated gaming rig, exceptional battery life, a laptop built for AI or for upgradeability.
 The MacBook PROLED and M6 MacBook Pro are now official, and these are already looking to be serious contenders for this guide. Stay tuned for our full reviews, and we’ll update you on the latest news. In the meantime, we've now seen what Nvidia RTX Spark laptops and Googlebooks can do, and have found just the ones worth buying.
 I'm here to guide you through the laptops worth buying right now. Read on for our expert advice, lab testing and hands-on reviews to help you find the laptop that's right for you.

 Should you buy the MacBook Air M5?
 The MacBook Air M5 has (unsurprisingly) taken over its M4 predecessor as the best MacBook and best laptop for most people reading this list, as it's hard to beat the mighty performance it offers at its cost. This time, though, its starting price is $100 more.
 Now starting at $1,299 for the 13-inch model and $1,499 for the 15-inch (but expect plenty of regular discounts), the latest MacBook Air may share that familiar lightweight, durable design, but its upgrades under the hood put its competition on notice. With faster M5 performance, double the base storage at 512GB, Wi-Fi 7 connectivity and longer battery life, this laptop ticks all the right boxes.
 Buy the MacBook Air M5 if
 ✅ You want a do-it-all laptop: With its M5 chip, along with its other notable upgrades, the latest MacBook Air takes its multitasking power to new heights, for web surfing, video editing and even some AAA gaming.
 ✅ You need a laptop that lasts: Now with 15 hours and 30 minutes of battery life, the M5 update makes the MacBook Air one of the longest-lasting laptops around, especially at its price. For those on the move or who don't want to rely on a charger, this laptop brings the stamina.
 Don't buy the MacBook Air M5 if
 ❌ If gaming is a priority: While the M5 is more than capable of playing demanding PC titles (like Resident Evil 4 Remake), it understandably isn't made for gaming. So don't think this will be your main gaming driver. 
❌ You already have an M4 or M3 MacBook Air: Despite the impressive performance gains the M5 delivers, along with the 512GB base storage and Wi-Fi 7 connectivity, this is more of a modest update. There's still plenty of software support left in those still-amazing laptops!
 Who is the MacBook Air M5 best for?
 💻 The MacBook Air M5 brings it home yet again, this time with notable upgrades that make this laptop better than ever. Yes, it's now $200 more for both the 13- and 15-inch models after Apple's price hikes, but this gets you a very welcome 512GB base storage, Apple N1 wireless chip for Wi-Fi 7 connectivity and longer battery life at over 15 hours.
 This isn't the upgrade to grab if you already have an M4, or even an M3, MacBook Air, but for frequent travelers, students and anyone who wants a reliable notebook that will be your trusty, lightweight companion, this is the best laptop to buy — especially when the inevitable discounts arrive to drop its bumped-up price tag.
 Read our full MacBook Air M5 review 
 Disclaimer 
 Thanks to Apple officially raising the price of MacBooks, the MacBook Air M5 is now priced from $1,299 (or $1,499 for the 15-inch model). That's a $200 price increase, and that's after the $100 surge in cost over the M4 model. While the price has gone up, we still rank it as the best laptop for most. We're constantly on the lookout for deals, so if we can find it at a lower price, be sure to grab it!

 Should you buy the MacBook Neo?
 Apple has changed the landscape of budget-friendly laptops with its MacBook Neo. It's almost strange to have a MacBook take the crown as the value laptop to beat, but for the performance, design and features it presents for $699 ($599 for education), it's clear this laptop raises the bar.
 The MacBook Neo comes with an A18 Pro chip, originally found in iPhones, but it still manages to run circles around Chromebooks and Windows laptops at similar prices and beats the MacBook Air M1. Plus, it comes with many of the perks of the MacBook Air, including a comfy keyboard and lightweight design (this time with fun colors). Trade-offs include paying extra for Touch ID, a lack of Thunderbolt and no keyboard backlight. But for its wallet-friendly price, this is no doubt the best value laptop around.
 Buy the MacBook Neo if
 ✅ You need a budget-friendly, versatile laptop: From day-to-day tasks to delivering long battery life, all wrapped up in a slim, lightweight design, the MacBook Neo makes for a fine machine for traveling professionals, students, families and anyone who just needs a laptop that won't break the bank.
 ✅ You want solid performance for less: Despite a lack of the usual M-series chipset, the MacBook Neo's A18 Pro can power through multiple tabs and apps without breaking a sweat. We noticed occasional lag every now and then, but hardly a deal-breaker. For this price, it's incredibly speedy.
 ✅ You like a splash of style: Who doesn't like a sturdy, all-aluminum laptop with fun colors to bring your at-home setup or office to life? Coming in Silver, Indigo, Blush and Citrus, the MacBook Neo is eye-catching.
 Don't buy the MacBook Neo if
 ❌ You want the perks of other MacBooks: The MacBook Neo doesn't come close to matching the performance of its Air or Pro siblings, which is expected, but it's a shame there's also no keyboard backlight, and Touch ID (with more storage) comes with a $100 price hump. Plus, 8GB of RAM isn't all that much.
 ❌ You need Thunderbolt connectivity: With Thunderbolt ports becoming the standard for many laptops, not seeing one in the MacBook Neo is a letdown, and limits the type of connections (to monitors, for instance) you can make.
 Who is the MacBook Neo best for?
 💻 The MacBook Neo is Apple's successful attempt at a budget laptop, and it ticks all the right boxes and makes the right (if annoying) trade-offs for it to be the value laptop for most.
 Now at $699, you'll get good performance from its impressive A18 Pro chip, long battery life that lasts over 13 hours, a vivid 13-inch display, the lightweight design of a MacBook Air with striking color options, great audio from its side speakers and the speediness of macOS. If you're fine with the sacrifices Apple has made, and only need an affordable machine for browsing the web, accessing apps, working on documents and more, you'll be very impressed with the MacBook Neo.
 Read our full Apple MacBook Neo review 
 Disclaimer 
 As with the rest of Apple's range of MacBooks, the MacBook Neo has seen a $100 price rise. While now priced from $699 (and $599 for students), it's still a great laptop for value at this cost, especially compared to its competition. However, we'll be sure to keep watch for any deals to help you save on this excellent budget-friendly machine.

 Should you buy the Dell XPS 14 (2026)?
 The Dell XPS 14 (2026) is the comeback we’ve all been waiting for. By ditching some of the controversial design aspects of previous models—along with the “Dell Premium” branding, the company has delivered a true MacBook Pro competitor. While it can get pricey, there’s a lot to like here.
 Starting at $1,599, you get a relatively thin and light machine that’s perfect for traveling with. Upgrades like a tandem OLED panel and a stronger Intel Panther Lake chip make this notebook even more enticing. Right now, it’s arguably the best Dell XPS laptop we’ve seen in years. Well, that and its bigger sibling, the Dell XPS 16 (2026) , which we also strongly recommend if you're after bigger (OLED) screen real estate.
 Buy the Dell XPS 14 (2026) if
 ✅ You want an ultraportable Windows laptop that’s as good for productivity as it is for gaming: Thanks to Panther Lake, this laptop can handle most of what you can throw at it.
 ✅ You need a long-lasting laptop: While the OLED model we tested only lasted 12 hours and 23 minutes, that’s still impressive endurance for a non-Snapdragon X Elite Windows machine. If you get the entry-level model, you can get over 20 hours of battery life, based on our testing.
 Don't buy the Dell XPS 14 (2026) if
 ❌ If you’re married to Apple: This one kind of goes without saying, but if you’re invested in the Apple ecosystem, any Windows laptop will be a hard sell. Also, an entry-level MacBook Pro M5 offers stronger performance and longer battery life than the higher-end $2,199 XPS 14 we reviewed.
 ❌ You need a microSD card: If you’re a creative, not having a microSD card slot could be a deal breaker. Keep that in mind when considering this laptop.
 Who is the Dell XPS 14 (2026) best for?
 💻 The Dell XPS 14 has a lot going for it, thanks to its new practical design, strong Panther Lake performance and efficiency, and tandem OLED upgrade option. While a return to form, it still retains some of the better aspects of the past, such as the glass touchpad and snappy keys. Dell wisely listened to its users and delivered a machine that’s worthy of the XPS branding.
 I’ve always been a fan of the XPS line, so I’m glad I can now recommend the latest model without adding a list of caveats. Beyond being a return to form, Dell has delivered an all-around fantastic machine that’s ready to go wherever you travel.
 If you’re a Windows user who wants a slick-looking and portable machine that’s as adept for work as it is for gaming, this one comes with my highest recommendation. Looking for a bigger screen? The Dell XPS 16 will impress just as much.

 Should you buy the Dell XPS 13 (2026)?
 The Dell XPS 13 (2026) is the rare budget Windows laptop that actually delivers long battery life and a sharp 2.5K touchscreen — two things you rarely see together at this price. In our battery test, it lasted 14 hours and 29 minutes, which is very impressive for a machine in this class. The screen isn’t just high-res on paper: that touchscreen adds a lot of value and makes this feel like a more expensive device than most competitors in the $700 range.
 Performance is another area where the XPS 13 punches above its weight. Our entry-level unit (8GB RAM, 512GB storage) scored 7,952 on Geekbench 6 multi-core, but what matters more is how it feels day to day. During a typical workflow —15 Chrome tabs open, YouTube streaming in the background — it never slowed it down. In short: you’re not paying for nothing here. This is the kind of value-to-performance ratio that reassures you your money’s well spent.
 Buy the Dell XPS 13 (2026) if
 ✅ You want fast, reliable day-to-day performance : The XPS 13 breezed through my typical multitasking — think 15 Chrome tabs and YouTube in the background — so routine work, browsing, and streaming won’t leave you frustrated.
 ✅ You need a laptop that lasts all day : In our battery test, the XPS 13 ran for 14 hours and 29 minutes of continuous web browsing — enough to get through classes or a full workday without plugging in.
 ✅ You carry your laptop everywhere : At just 2.2 pounds, with a sturdy aluminum chassis, the XPS 13 is genuinely comfortable to haul between rooms, classes or commutes.
 Don't buy the Dell XPS 13 (2026) if
 ❌ You need a sharp webcam: For those who go on video calls often, know that the XPS 13's 1080p webcam can make you look blurry and washed out. It's serviceable, but not the best around.
 ❌ You want plenty of ports: With only two USB-C ports and no headphone jack, the XPS 13 doesn't give you a lot to play around with, especially if you want to connect extra peripherals, like a mouse, keyboard and more.
 Who is the Dell XPS 13 (2026) best for?
 💻 The Dell XPS 13 (2026) has value written all over it, and it makes it an easy recommendation as the best budget Windows laptop to buy. At under $700/£700, this laptop offers reliable performance for everyday tasks, an ultra-lightweight and thin design that's anything but cheap and all-day battery life at over 14 hours.
 If you’re a price-conscious Windows user, like a student, remote worker or anyone who needs a dependable daily driver, the Dell XPS 13 gets the basics right, and then some. Just don’t expect workstation-level performance or gaming chops, and you’ll find a lot to love for the money.

 Should you buy the Asus ROG Zephyrus G14?
 The Asus ROG Zephyrus G14 is my personal favorite gaming laptop you can buy — primarily because it doesn’t forget about the “laptop” part like a lot of gaming systems do.
 This refreshed model packs a ton of power into that sleek MacBook Pro-esque aluminum shell in the form of the latest AMD CPU and Nvidia RTX 50-series GPU combo. But the more things change, the more they (fortunately) stay the same, thanks to that gorgeous CNC-milled utilitarian aesthetic and a mesmerizing OLED display.
 If you need more raw horsepower dedicated to gaming, there are more performant options, and I recommend you check out our best gaming laptops list. But for a better balance of all elements that still delivers big on power, the Zephyrus G14 is a near-perfect pick.
 Buy the Asus ROG Zephyrus G14 if
 ✅ You want a beasty gaming machine: AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 + Nvidia GeForce RTX 5080 makes for a monstrous pairing of power. Combine that with improved cooling and DLSS 4, and you can run the latest AAA games at over 140 FPS in max settings.
 ✅ You don’t want other people to know you have a gaming laptop: The standard gaming laptop design is pretty cringe. I always feel uncomfortable pulling one out. But the Zephyrus G14’s tastefully utilitarian CNC-milled aluminum construction looks fantastically subtle from every angle.
 ✅ You care about a good screen: That 3K OLED panel is a real marvel to look at — presenting all your favorite games with a real HDR quality that pushes impressive color and a deep contrast ratio.
 Don't buy the Asus ROG Zephyrus G14 if
 ❌ Battery life is a chief concern: This is more a problem I’ve found with gaming laptops as a whole rather than this specific model. But it’s worth noting, as the stamina levels of such highly demanding internals does drop the battery life in day-to-day use to below 7 hours of casual use.
 ❌ Webcam quality matters: The 1080p webcam remains unchanged from the Zephyrus G14 last year, which means you’re getting quite the grainy picture that struggles with low lighting.
 Who is the Asus ROG Zephyrus G14 best for?
 💻 The Asus ROG Zephyrus G14 is a fantastic gaming laptop that kept me entertained across 5,000 miles of travel, balancing performance and portability perfectly. The OLED display makes all your gaming look incredibly colorful and immersive, the speakers have been improved, and it’s impressively thin and lightweight.
 This is the best gaming laptop for folks who actually want to take their gaming laptops with them on occasion. Most gaming laptops are so big, heavy and poorly optimized that they're basically desktop replacements, since they're best left on your desk for their entire lifespan.
 Not so with the Zephyrus; while battery life while gaming still isn't amazing, this thing fits in a backpack fairly easily and doesn't look out of place in a coffee shop or classroom, so you can take it to school and sneak in some gaming time at lunch. It's the best laptop for anyone who wants a gaming laptop that can double as a work device in a pinch.

 Should you buy the Framework Laptop?
 When it came out we called the Framework Laptop the Anti-MacBook because it's everything Apple doesn't do in laptops: repairable, upgradable and respectful of your rights as an owner.
 I was initially excited about those promises but dubious the company could deliver on them without some glaring sacrifices. But now that I’ve used one myself, I’m happy to report the Framework Laptop is as good as advertised.

 Buy the Framework Laptop if
 ✅ You care about your right to repair: I've never seen a laptop that's easier to open up, fiddle around with and put back together. No other laptop on the market can match the Framework in this regard, so if you care about being able to repair and upgrade your laptop, this is the one for you.
 ✅ You're plagued by port envy: On most laptops, the ports it comes with are all you get. The Framework is different: you can change what ports it sports by buying hot-swappable Expansion Cards that you plug into 4 slots on the bottom of the laptop, and each can have one port on it. So you can swap out 2 USB-C and 2 USB-A ports for 1 USB-C, 1 USB-A, a DisplayPort out and an Ethernet jack, for example.
 ✅ You like a tall screen: The 3:2 display ratio of the Framework's screen feels a bit taller than the displays found on most laptops, and it's great for working with "tall" things like long documents, emails, coding projects and more.
 Don't buy the Framework Laptop if

This is a feature, not a problem, but it can unnerve new owners.
 ❌ You don't want to pay extra for ports: The Framework offers unrivaled port versatility thanks to its Expansion Card system, but it does require buying a handful of Cards for all the ports and other options you want, some of which could be easily lost or misplaced.
 Who is the Framework Laptop best for?
 💻 The Framework Laptop is a remarkable piece of tech. It's a great laptop for getting work done, but more than that, it's a statement of purpose, a clear example that every other laptop maker could be building and selling us more repairable, sustainable laptops if they cared to as much as Framework does.
 While it can be a bit daunting to open and upgrade, this is the ideal laptop for DIY fans, right-to-repair fanatics and anyone who wants to take a little more ownership of their tech. It's also an ideal laptop for curious students who love to tinker and take things apart. It's a fantastic investment if you care about your right to repair and upgrade your own laptop.

 Read our full Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3x review 
 View Deal 
 Asus ROG Flow Z13 : $2,299 at Amazon (★★★★☆ ½ ) 
Asus' ROG Flow Z13 is a marvel of engineering that delivers decent PC gaming power on a lovely 2.5K mini-LED display in an ultra-thin 2-in-1 design. That means you can use it as a gaming laptop or tablet, and the AMD Ryzen AI Max 390 chip inside delivers gaming performance roughly equivalent to a dedicated Nvidia GeForce RTX 4070 laptop GPU. However, the fact that it's more expensive than the ROG Zephyrus G14 and delivers slightly worse gaming performance keeps it from claiming the best gaming laptop honors.
 Read our full Asus ROG Flow Z13 review 
 ▲ Back to the top 
 Latest news 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) There will always be another laptop coming down the line, and we're here to keep you updated on the latest machines to put on your radar. Here's what's coming up:
 Apple’s “Pro and Tell” event finally revealed what we’ve all been waiting for: the MacBook PROLED XDR . Boasting an OLED touchscreen and M5 Pro/Max, this looks to be the ultimate machine for pro users. However, there’s also the next-gen MacBook Pro M6 , and that’s already looking to impress, considering the Mac mini M6 delivers fast performance. The MacBook Ultra will be available on November 6 with prices starting at $2,999, while the MacBook Pro M6 will be available on November 6 with prices starting at $1,999.
 Qualcomm announced its new Snapdragon C chip , set to bring a new wave of budget laptops priced around $300 to $400. Targeted at students, families and small businesses, laptops with Snapdragon C are made for general tasks, such as web browsing, video streaming and productivity. But we can also expect an integrated NPU for on-device AI tasks. We can expect the first Snapdragon C laptops from HP, Lenovo, and Acer, with one of the first being the Acer Aspire Go 15. We expect these to arrive sometime later this year.
 ▲ Back to the top 
 Best Laptops: Frequently Asked Questions 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Should I buy a MacBook, Windows laptop or a Chromebook?
 Buy a MacBook if you are comfortable using Macs or are already embedded in the Apple ecosystem. While macOS is not as robust as Windows when it comes to gaming, many people find it easy to use and it's tightly integrated with Apple's other products, so your iPhone, iPad and AirPods will seamlessly work with your Mac.
 Buy a Windows 11 laptop if you need access to the widest selection of apps, are not tied down to any particular ecosystem, want the best gaming experience and are looking for the broadest selection of laptop designs. Only Windows laptops come with features like touchscreens, high-speed displays or the option to transform into a tablet. However, they typically have worse battery life than MacBooks. 
 Buy a Chromebook or Googlebook if your work and entertainment needs revolve entirely around a browser, Android or Gemini AI. If everything you do is within a Chrome browser or Google apps, then a Chromebook or higher-tier Googlebook is the most direct way to get there. Just be aware you'll be limited without internet — ChromeOS and Googlebook OS are robust operating systems, but without internet access, they can't do much.
 How much should I spend on a good laptop?
 Spend enough to match your workload, rather than paying for power or features you will not use. The best budget laptops can handle browsing, documents and streaming; mainstream laptops offer a better balance of portability and multitasking; and premium machines make sense for demanding creative work, gaming or maximum battery life.
 Our budget picks, the MacBook Neo and Dell XPS 13 , suit everyday tasks, while models such as the MacBook Air M5 and Dell XPS 14 are stronger all-round choices. Gaming and professional creative laptops cost more because they need faster components, more memory and better cooling. Prices and discounts change regularly, so compare the current configurations and avoid treating a temporary deal as a permanent price point.
 How much RAM do I need?
 For a modern laptop, 16GB of RAM is a sensible target for smooth everyday use and multitasking. It gives web browsers, office apps and background processes more room to run together, and is a better long-term choice than 8GB where the budget allows. Of course, with the RAM crisis , this is getting trickier, but with the right laptop, 8GB of RAM can take you far (as the MacBook Neo and Dell XPS 13 have shown us). 
 Choose more memory if you edit video, work with 3D projects, run demanding creative software, stream while gaming or regularly keep many intensive apps open. We recommend 32GB as a minimum for especially heavy 3D animation and streaming workloads. RAM is often not upgradeable on a laptop after purchase, so select the configuration you expect to need over the laptop’s useful life.
 What is an SSD, and how much storage do I need?
 An SSD is fast, flash-based storage that holds your operating system, apps and files; 256GB is a workable starting point, while 512GB gives most people more comfortable room. Unlike older mechanical hard drives, SSDs have no moving parts and are generally quicker and more robust for everyday laptop use.
 Choose 512GB or more if you keep large photo libraries or offline files on the laptop. Cloud storage and external SSDs can reduce the need for built-in capacity, but they are less convenient when travelling. For gaming and video projects, we suggest getting 1TB or more, as these large files can take up a lot of space fast. 
 What battery life should I look for in a laptop?
 Look for a laptop with enough battery life we've tested to cover your normal day away from a socket, rather than relying only on a manufacturer’s claim. Around a full work or study day is a useful goal for many buyers, but the right target depends on your workload, screen settings and how often you travel. As a good rule of thumb, if a laptop lasts over 10 hours, it's doing a good job. 
 In our testing, the MacBook Air M5 lasted more than 15 hours, the Dell XPS 13 more than 14 hours, and the MacBook Pro 16-inch M5 Pro more than 21 hours in its battery test. Gaming is much more demanding: the ROG Zephyrus G14 records far shorter gaming endurance, so plan to carry a charger for intensive use.
 Which accessories should I buy?
 Start with accessories that improve comfort and connectivity: a laptop stand, a mouse and, if required, a USB hub or dock. A stand can raise the screen to a more comfortable height, while a mouse is often more comfortable for long work sessions than relying on a trackpad. Check out our guide to the best mouse for more options. 
 Check your laptop’s ports and charging requirements before buying a hub or dock, especially with slim ultraportables that may offer only USB-C connections. A hub can add useful connections for displays, storage, keyboards and wired networking, but it must support the standards and power delivery your laptop needs. Buy additional accessories only for a genuine use case, such as one of the best monitors as an extra screen to have, a travel case or extra storage.
 ▲ Back to the top 
 How to choose the best laptop for you 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) To help you make choosing the right laptop for you easier, here's our expert advice on the key factors and features for different needs.
 Work and productivity: If your first priority is having an easy-to-carry PC you can use to answer email, prep documents and get work done on the go, you want a modern ultraportable that's light, comfy to use and offers great battery life. I generally recommend the MacBook Air M5 (macOS) or the Dell XPS 14 (Windows 11) for this, since they're both light, capable and long-lasting. You'll also find the Lenovo Googlebook 15 makes for an excellent lightweight addition. If you're technical and like the idea of upgrading and repairing your own laptop, I wholeheartedly recommend you check out the Framework Laptop instead, since you can modify and upgrade it for as long as you own it, in a way that no other laptop can match.
 Gaming: If you plan to spend a lot of time gaming, you want a laptop with a speedy CPU, a discrete laptop graphics card and plenty of RAM. If you plan to play at higher than 60 frames per second, a screen with a high refresh rate is also critical. Personally, I recommend the Asus ROG Zephyrus G14 since it satisfies all these requirements while remaining pretty portable, but if you adore macOS, the MacBook Pro M5 is also pretty good for gaming if you restrict yourself to games optimized for Apple Silicon. But now, you can also play the latest titles with a laptop like the Dell XPS 14 , Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra and Asus ProArt P16 with RTX Spark.
 Creative work: If you plan to do a lot of 3D work, audio/video editing or demanding content creation, you will want a laptop with a powerful CPU, a discrete GPU (or powerful integrated graphics) and plenty of RAM to handle demanding workloads. In that sense, you want something like a gaming laptop (but ideally with better battery life and lighter weight), and you also want a sharp, color-accurate screen. This is why I generally recommend the MacBook Pro M5 , Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra and Asus ProArt P16 for such uses.
 Casual use: If you just need a laptop for basic writing, browsing the web and binge-watching YouTube or your favorite shows, you can save yourself a lot of money with a budget-friendly laptop. I recommend the MacBook Neo if you prefer macOS, the Dell XPS 13 for Windows or the Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14 if you're okay with a Chromebook and have reliable access to Wi-Fi (because Chromebooks can't do much without an internet connection).
 ▲ Back to the top 
 How we test laptops 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) In our never-ending quest to find the best laptops, I put every computer we test through a barrage of synthetic and real-world tests to benchmark how well it performs compared to the manufacturer's claims, and compare how good it is relative to the competition.
 These tests include, but are not limited to: measuring the average brightness and color quality of each laptop's display using our in-house colorimeter, using a heat gun to measure the heat generated by the laptop after 15 minutes of strenuous work, and using a mix of real-world and synthetic benchmarks to test how well a laptop performs at various day-to-day tasks.
 I put all laptops through the Geekbench CPU performance benchmark tests as well as various 3DMark tests to measure graphics capabilities. I also run a file transfer test to measure how fast a machine's hard drive is, a video transcoding test to gauge how well a laptop can cut video and a custom battery test that has the machine browse the internet over Wi-Fi until it runs out of juice.
 There are also gaming benchmarks that I use — testing a basic game like Sid Meier's Civilization VI: Gathering Storm to gauge how good it is at running games compared to other laptops. I use this old game because it runs on a wide variety of laptops across different prices, sizes and operating systems, so it's great for comparing performance.
 Of course, when testing dedicated gaming laptops, I run benchmarks for many more demanding and popular games, including Assassin's Creed Shadows, Cyberpunk 2077 and Black Myth: Wukong . For more information on our testing process, check out our guide to how we test .

 You've got yourself a MacBook Pro, and you're here to find a display that will act as the perfect companion for your desk setup. Well, after connecting Apple's Pro laptop to the latest screens that land on our desks, we've done the testing and found the best monitors for MacBook Pro.
 Apple's 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pros already come equipped with amazing Liquid Retina XDR displays, but to extend your workspace with monitors that match the rich, colorful visuals and high pixel density those screens offer raises the bar for your setup. That's why my team of experts and I have done extensive hands-on testing for picture quality, color accuracy, connectivity and more for each monitor to help you find the right fit for your desk.
 Right now, we highly recommend the Philips 27E3U7903 as the best monitor for MacBook Pro for most, as this 5K beauty ticks all the right boxes and is far less expensive than Apple's Studio Display (even though that is still a great choice). We've got more choices to put on your radar, so if you're ready to give your MacBook Pro the monitor it deserves, our guide will point you in the right direction.
 Looking for other displays from Apple's lineup of Macs? Check out our guides on the best monitors for Mac mini and the best monitors for Mac Studio , too.

 Reasons to avoid

 The Philips 27E3U7903 takes the crown as our top pick for MacBook Pro users who want a monitor that nails modern connectivity and delivers a true high-res experience without the Apple tax. In our testing, we found it needs to be excellent across the board to justify its premium price, and the combination of practical features and 5K clarity gets it most of the way there.
 Connectivity is where the 27E3U7903 shines. With HDMI 2.1, a Thunderbolt 4 port delivering 96W of Power Delivery (enough to fully charge a MacBook Pro), plus additional Thunderbolt, USB-C, and USB-A ports, it handles single-cable docking, peripheral charging, and daisy chaining with ease. We found the built-in KVM switch and multi-port options made switching between devices and tidying up desk clutter genuinely seamless.
 On the visual front, you’re getting a 5K (5120 x 2880) panel using IPS Black tech, meaning crisp, retina-style sharpness for macOS, vibrant colors, and a punchy backlight. In hands-on use, the panel’s vibrancy and power stood out, making it suitable for everything from spreadsheets to creative work, even if it won’t quite match Apple on calibration out of the box.
 Yes, the Apple Studio Display still wins for build quality and Mac integration, but the Philips matches its resolution and undercuts it on price. So you aren’t paying for the logo.
 If you’re looking for a premium-feeling, high-resolution monitor that offers practical one-cable MacBook Pro docking, the 27E3U7903 is a strong choice. You’ll give up some of Apple’s design polish and factory calibration, but for most users after ports, clarity, and versatility, it’s the best all-rounder we’ve tested.

 The BenQ GW2486TC Eye-Care Monitor is as budget-friendly as it gets for MacBook Pro users who just want a reliable desktop screen with a single-cable USB-C connection.
 You get 65W USB-C power delivery (enough for lighter MacBooks and most workdays), a 24-inch 1080p IPS panel, and a measured 99% sRGB color coverage. That simple yet effective combination delivers sharp enough text and reasonably accurate colors for routine tasks and light creative work.
 We used this monitor daily for a month, pairing it with various laptops and running through everything from spreadsheets to streaming media, and it made for a great screen companion. For one, the stand offers 130mm of height adjustment, 45-degree swivel, and 90-degree pivot, so it’s easy to dial in a comfortable setup. Secondly, the OSD menu is straightforward, and those eye-care modes are a genuine plus for long sessions, especially if your workday stretches late.
 Of course, you’re making clear trade-offs versus pricier options. The BenQ’s 65W power delivery is well below its 90W competition, and won’t keep a 16-inch MacBook Pro charged under heavy load. You’re also giving up 4K resolution and Thunderbolt, features you’ll others like the Apple Studio Display.
 For basic office use, though, the savings are real. If you’re after a clean, simple MacBook Pro setup on a tight budget, the GW2486TC covers the basics better than anything else we’ve tested at this price.

 A quantum dot 4K OLED display with "spectacular" picture quality per reviewer Collin Probst's testing, is the obvious star of the show. It's a superb panel for photo and video editing, and lends itself well for website design. A detachable shader also help reinforce this monitor's professional chops, but its gets plenty bright without needing the shade, according to Probst.
 Dell has a stellar reputation for making great displays for professionals, so this 32-inch OLED display's quality isn't a huge surprise. What is nice is that the monitor can do a lot via a single Thunderbolt port with power delivery, handy to plug into the somewhat restrained port selection of MacBook Pro laptops. But it also has a host of other ports, from HDMI 2.1 ports to USB-C and more, meaning you can build a comprehensive creator-centric desktop set up around it.
 Over to Probst to have the final word: "If you know you're looking for an absurdly nice monitor because you are a video editor, a photo editor, or a content creator in some way, and you need a high-quality one, then absolutely make sure you check this one out."

 While the Dell monitor above displaces the Asus ProArt PA32UCDM from its spot on this list, it's still a great monitor for creators.
 You get a 32-inch 4K OLED panel delivers a sprawling workspace and crisp detail, making it ideal for photo editors, video colorists, designers – you name it. The display also offers 99% DCI-P3 coverage and a decent range of hardware calibration tools, including 3D LUT, ProArt calibration, and CalMAN Autocal,
 During our hands-on time, the PA32UCDM impressed us with its exceptional display quality. HDR video content in particular absolutely zings, with highlights that leap off the screen and a vibrancy that’s a clear step up from typical IPS or even WOLED panels. So it's well worth a look if the Dell UltraSharp U3226Q is a little to pricey for you.

 It wouldn't really be a list of monitors for the MacBook Pro without the Apple Studio Display, as it's still a fantastic choice that makes sense for most. No, it's not the best 5K display around, but for a monitor that perfectly pairs with the MacBook Pro, it’s pretty hard to beat. It features Apple's signature Retina-style levels of pixel density (218 pixels per inch, to be precise), with fonts and images appearing crisp and clean. And, of course, it has that excellent Apple style and build quality.
 Connectivity is a definite strong point for the Studio Display, thanks to the Thunderbolt port with 96W Power Delivery for charging your MacBook Pro. There are also three USB-C ports for peripherals. On the display side, the panel has 98% coverage of the DCI-P3 gamut and a strong peak brightness of 600 nits.
 Elsewhere, we especially liked the excellent 12MP ultra-wide webcam, which features a 122-degree field of view, a studio-quality three-mic array, and six speakers. Speaking of which, we found sound quality was far superior to pretty much any conventional PC monitor.
 Limitations, then, would be the price. It’s still pretty expensive even for a 5K monitor, and that doesn’t include a height-adjustable stand. The 60Hz refresh rate, while not essential, can’t match that of the 120Hz on the MacBook Pro 14-inch and 16-inch laptops. And black levels and contrast are nowhere near what a monitor with local dimming or an OLED panel can achieve.
 Still, for a 5K display with Retina-style pixel density and tight integration with your MacBook Pro, there are few other options.

 Best monitor for MacBook Pro: FAQs 
 (Image credit: Acer // Future) What is the best resolution for monitors with a MacBook Pro?
 The MacBook Pro is Apple's machine for creators, and that means having excellent visuals for photo and video editing, 3D creative work, and more. To make the most out of what you work on, 4K (3840 x 2160) resolution is the way to go. That said, if you're using your MacBook Pro for anything else, like spreadsheets, writing documents or even coding, you'll be just fine with even a 1080p display. If you're after the highest pixel density, though, 5K and upwards is what you're after. 
 What Power Delivery should the monitor have to charge my MacBook Pro?
 You'll see many monitors with Thunderbolt/USB-C Power Delivery (PD). This means you can plug your MacBook Pro into the monitor and it will charge the laptop while in use. 
 However, the right choice depends on your MacBook Pro's model and CPU. Check out the table below to see which one is right for your laptop.

 Are there any specific connectivity options that I should look for in a monitor for my MacBook Pro?
 The best monitors for a MacBook Pro will feature USB-C and/or Thunderbolt connectivity. These allow slick, single-cable connectivity that covers charging the MacBook, driving the display, and connecting peripherals. 
 Outside of that, you can find a monitor with a built-in USB-C hub that opens up several ports through the single USB-C used to send video to your monitor. Depending on the monitor, sometimes this can also be used to charge your MacBook Pro.
 Are there any monitors that are specifically designed for use with the MacBook Pro?
 Some monitors, such as the Apple Studio Display and Apple Pro Display XDR, are explicitly designed for use with Apple devices and mirror the wide color P3 gamut and Liquid Retina Display. 
 However, many high-quality monitors from other brands are also compatible with the MacBook Pro. Some monitors will work better with the MacBook Pro than others, but generally, any even semi-recent monitor will be compatible in one way or another with a MacBook Pro.
 How to choose the best monitor for MacBook Pro 
 When choosing which monitor is best for your MacBook Pro, there are a few specs and details you'll want to check.
 Not everyone will need the same specifications. For example, if you're mostly working with office apps, you may not need the broader color space coverage that's required for image or video editing. However you use your monitor, here's what we recommend looking out for.
 Resolution : macOS loves high-resolution displays. The more pixels, the better for rendering nice, clean fonts and providing plenty of image detail. Apple's own desktop displays, the Apple Pro Display XDR and Studio Display, have what's known as Retina pixel density. In practice, that means over 200 pixels per inch (PPI), which matches the screens in the MacBook Pro. Very few non-Apple displays can match that pixel density, but a 27-inch 4K display with 163 pixels per inch is a good baseline.
 Connectivity : USB-C or Thunderbolt with Power Delivery is the bare minimum when it comes to connectivity. We'd recommend at least 65W of power delivery and ideally 90W-plus for keeping your MacBook Pro fully powered. A USB hub with plenty of USB-A and USB-C ports is very desirable, too. Additional inputs like HDMI can be handy, and an Ethernet port can be useful for some office environments. The ability to daisy chain a second monitor is also an interesting option, as is a KVM switch if you're sharing the display with a second computer.
 HDR versus SDR support: HDR is a tricky technology. Many workflows don't require it. But it is becoming more widespread. A display with HDR capability tends to also offer increased colour coverage and generally improve image quality. However, the technologies that enable HDR rendering vary hugely, and some displays are much more effective than others. For that reason, unless you know your workflows require full HDR support, we recommend focusing on getting a display with good SDR performance. If it happens to also offer some HDR capability, great. But for most users, HDR probably isn't a top priority.
 Build quality and extras: It's easy to obsess over specifications like resolution and HDR performance. But the overall quality of a display and feature set can make a big difference, too. If you're paying big bucks, it's nice to have a display that feels worth the money and looks good with your laptop. Likewise, superficially lesser features like good speakers, a great webcam and a microphone array can make a big difference to the overall usability of a monitor. Having features like that built in can also help to reduce desk clutter and simplify docking and connectivity. For more extras, we've reviewed the best MacBook Pro accessories .
 How we test the best monitors for MacBook Pro 
 (Image credit: Future) Our expert team of reviewers has tested a massive range of displays, including the best monitors for photo editing and the best monitors for video editing . So, we're experienced at knowing what to look out for to help you find the best dual monitor set-up to go with your laptop.
 A decent monitor for your MacBook Pro isn't going to be cheap. So, you want to know you're making the right choice. That's why we test each display extensively. That starts with performance assessments of various aspects of image quality.
 That includes brightness, refresh rate, and pixel response. We also consider colour accuracy, viewing angles, contrast, HDR performance, latency, and last but by no means least, resolution and pixel density. Display tech is increasingly varied and complex, what with new technologies like HDR, mini-LED backlights, and OLED panels revolutionising the industry. So, we keep on top of all of that for you, helping you to understand the difference between a few edge-lit dimming zones and a real full-array deal
 Crucially, we also assess how well a display works with macOS. Once connected to a MacBook Pro, does it offer a full range of optimised scaling options, for instance? Next up is connectivity. We consider the range of ports on offer and whether single-cable docking with power delivery is included, along with USB hubs and other features like Ethernet, a KVM switch, and display daisy chaining.
 We also consider any extra features like webcams and speakers. In theory, they can add significant value. But if they're not done well, you're probably just paying for things you'll hardly ever use. You might even end up paying twice if you find you need to buy a dedicated webcam or speakers.
 Next up, there's build quality, design, and ergonomics. A monitor that looks great on the desk with your MacBook Pro is important. But good build quality matters, too. When you are investing a lot of money, you want a display to not just look good, but feel good and last the test of time.
 Then there's ergonomics. At a minimum, a robust and stable stand with a good range of adjustability, including height and tilt, is important. The ability to rotate into portrait mode can be handy, too.
 Of course, how all of those factors fit into the overall value proposition is the final measure. The MacBook Pro is a demanding machine. So, you're not going to get the best out of it with a budget display. But you can also spend a lot of money and not necessarily get a better display solution. We'll help you work out what's worth the money and what costs plenty but doesn't improve your macOS experience.
 Find out more about our process in our guide on how we test, review, and rate on TechRadar Pro: professional and business monitors .

 If you get yourself one of the best MacBooks, know that you aren't just getting a sleek, reliable machine, no matter the model; you're also choosing one of the best laptops on the market. I know, as I've been using a MacBook as my daily driver for years.
 We here at Tom's Guide have put together this guide to help you find the best one for your needs, after reviewing all the latest MacBooks for nearly 20 years.
 The MacBook Air M5 is an easy recommendation as the best MacBook for most people. All-day battery life and even better specs under the hood compared to previous models make it a winner, despite the bump in price. But if you're all about affordability, the MacBook Neo is an exemplary budget laptop for the price. It's a win for students, first-time Mac users and, well, anyone looking for plenty of value.
 If you're a creative pro and need the extra performance, I’d steer you toward either the MacBook Pro M5 or, for the monster GPU to nail professional-grade video edits and AI, the MacBook Pro M5 Pro . But hold on! During Apple’s “Pro and Tell” event , the long-rumored MacBook PROLED and next-gen M6 MacBook Pro were finally revealed, and we got hands-on time with both laptops. Once we’ve finished testing, we’ll let you know how these new MacBooks perform, and whether they’re right for you. Find out more in our FAQs .
 For MacBook owners and first-time buyers, you'll want to know that macOS Golden Gate has arrived, and it's available to download and install now . This brings a bigger focus to the all-new Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features. It's not a big update, but to make the most of Siri AI, it's worth downloading. For more hands-on testing and expert advice, this guide will help you find the best MacBook for your needs.
 The best MacBooks you can buy today
 Why you can trust Tom's Guide
 Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

 What Our Reviewer Says 
 Tony Polanco 
 Senior Computing Writer 
 The MacBook Air 13-inch M5 offers nice upgrades over the M4 version while keeping the same sleek design, vibrant display, and long battery life. M5 performance impresses, and the doubled 512GB storage and better wireless connectivity are nice bonuses. Yes, it costs an extra $100 (and an extra $200 after Apple's price hikes ) for most of the same features as the M4 model. Still, the MacBook Air M5 is a fantastic laptop for most folks, especially anyone looking for a premium notebook (that you'll definitely find for under $1,000 during a sale). 
 Who is the MacBook Air M5 13-inch for?
 This is the go-to MacBook for most folks. Why? The MacBook Air M5 13-inch brings even faster performance under the hood thanks to the M5 chip, which also results in even greater battery life at over 15 hours. That's all wrapped up in the familiar yet fantastic, sleek, lightweight design, especially with the 13-inch model. Aside from those who already have an M4, or even an M3, MacBook Air, this is hands down not just the MacBook, but also the laptop to beat.
 Why is it the best overall MacBook?
 As with its predecessor, the MacBook Air M5 comes out on top because it ticks all the right boxes. Premium performance for a laptop under $1,500 (and even less when those discounts start pouring in)? Check. Faster M5 power for seamless multitasking, especially for web surfing, video editing and even demanding gaming? It's got it. Now offering over 15 hours of battery life, Wi-Fi 7 connectivity and an upgraded 512GB base storage? You know it. It's got it all for most.

 (Image credit: Paul Antill - Tom's Guide) Should I buy a MacBook now or wait for the next model?
 We can expect a new set of next-gen Air, Pro and now even Neo MacBook models annually. However, don't feel you need to upgrade every year.
 That being said, no one wants to buy a current-generation MacBook only for Apple to launch the next-gen model the next day (I would feel that pain!). To avoid that, here’s a look at MacBooks (potentially) coming up.
 MacBook PROLED XDR : It's Apple's first touchscreen MacBook, and it's something to behold. It's mega powerful, and the screen is unreasonably beautiful. It's packing an M5 Pro or Max chip, and it's lighter than the standard M6 model. You'll also find higher RAM configurations. Just be ready to pay a mighty price for one.
 MacBook Pro M6 : There are a couple of key upgrades here of note: The first is the new M6 chip, which promises much speedier performance and better AI capability. 24 hours of battery life sounds good too, and there's now a Nanotexture option for a glare-free screen. 
 Each jump for Apple's laptops is a more modest upgrade with the same design and display. The improvements tend to come under the hood, but unless you're jumping from, say, a MacBook Pro M1 to a MacBook Pro M5, don't expect huge leaps in performance. 
 Apple's latest lineup of MacBooks is the best around, but don't worry about upgrading if you only got the previous year's model. However, when a revamp is expected, or a new launch is right around the corner, it's often best to hold off on buying the current-gen MacBook you had your eye on. 
 That's because you'll get the latest and greatest MacBook right when it launches, and for (hopefully) the same price you'd pay for the model that would instantly be considered the "last-gen" model. It will prolong how many more years of use you'd get out of it, but there's also something to be said about saving on an earlier MacBook; although expect these to be "renewed" models at major retailers. 
 In any case, if we're hearing about a MacBook launch that's just around the corner, or a fully revamped model, your best bet is to wait to upgrade.

 What is macOS?
 macOS is Apple's own operating system for its lineup of Macs, and it's an intuitive, seamless OS that tightly integrates with the rest of the Cupertino tech giant's products, like the iPhone and iPad. 
 Every year, macOS gets a major update, bringing new features and tweaks to check out. Right now, we're on macOS Golden Gate (macOS 27), which is available to upgrade to now . This is mainly focused on bringing Siri AI to the forefront, so it is largely the same as the previous macOS Tahoe (macOS 26). 
 Here's what to expect in the latest macOS 27 update:
 Siri AI and Apple Intelligence: Apple's rebuilt take on AI is integrated throughout the system, with contextual awareness, conversational capabilities and improved natural-language support. For example, through the Siri AI app in the Dock, Menu or Spotlight, it can help write and proofread drafts from scratch, find a PDF invoice in one of your emails in Spotlight and use Visual Intelligence to answer questions based on what's on screen. This works in a similar way to ChatGPT and Google Gemini .
 Liquid Glass Slider: The design overhaul introduced in macOS Tahoe will now be easier to customize, with sliders to change the opacity and color of windows, tiles and apps, along with edges of apps now being more defined to stand out more in the background.
 Spatial Reframing: As with iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 , Spatial Reframing is a new feature in the Photos app that lets you reframe existing photos and adjust the perspective however you like. It's a great tool to have if you're looking for a different angle, and it can now be done on macOS. 
 Which MacBooks support Apple Intelligence? 
 Back in 2024, Apple released the initial version of Apple Intelligence for Macs, iPads and iPhones. The launch has been, well, rocky to say the least. But now, we're getting a completely built-from-the-ground-up Apple Intelligence in the form of Siri AI , coming with macOS Golden Gate. 
 This brings smarter suggestions across Apple's range of apps, such as scheduling an event or reminder in the Calendar app after someone messages about an upcoming appointment, understanding what's on your screen with Visual Intelligence, analyzing files and bringing up what's most relevant, and more. 
 Every MacBook on this list will meet these requirements, touting a Neural Engine on the chipset and over 16GB of RAM. However, MacBooks with Intel chips will not support Apple Intelligence (i.e., those sold in 2019 and earlier).
 Should I buy a MacBook Air or a MacBook Pro?
 Buy a MacBook Air for everyday work, study, web browsing, light creative tasks and the easiest portability. Buy a MacBook Pro when you need higher sustained performance, more ports or a higher-end display. The MacBook Air M5 is our best overall choice because it combines strong everyday performance with a thin, light design and long battery life.
 Choose the Pro if you regularly edit video, compile code, work in demanding creative apps or even game during your usual week. Even with the MacBook Pro M5 , its cooling fan helps it sustain heavy workloads for longer, and it has a better selection of ports. 
 How much RAM and storage do I need in a MacBook?
 It's important to choose enough memory and storage for the work you expect to do over the laptop’s lifetime, because both are fixed once bought (you can always ad an external SSD for storage, though). For browsing, documents and streaming, a base configuration of 16GB and 512GB is enough to get through work tasks, video editing work and light gaming. For frequent multitasking, creative apps, development work or longer ownership, prioritise more memory above all.
 Storage needs depend on whether you keep large photo, video or project libraries locally. The current MacBook Air M5 starts with 512GB now, and the MacBook Neo offers 512GB for an extra $100/£100, which gives many buyers more flexibility than its previous smaller capacities. 
 How to choose the best MacBook for you 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) As of 2026, there are three types to choose from:
 MacBook Neo: The budget pick that boasts more than enough power for browsing the web with multiple tabs and handling apps, wrapped up in a compact, sturdy frame with a splash of fun colors.
 MacBook Air: The go-to option for everyone that ticks all the boxes for everyday productivity, creative work, web browsing, some light gaming and the like in an ultra-thin and light form factor.
 MacBook Pro: The powerhouse for those who want to get into more demanding work like video editing, coding, music production or even gaming.
 Each comes with its own set of strengths, but it all depends on your needs and budget. Here's a breakdown of what to check out:
 Performance: The transition to Apple Silicon breathed new life into the MacBook lineup — pairing seriously impressive performance with peak power efficiency and downright bafflingly low operating temperatures (even under max load). Of course, the question of how much of that face-melting speed you need comes down to individual use cases. Not really doing much beyond casual productivity? The MacBook Neo is perfect. Need a little more? Bump up to the MacBook Air M5 . If you're a power user with creative tasks, the M5 MacBook Pros are the way to go.
 Graphics and gaming: If you want to work by day and play by night on your MacBook, anything with an M3 chip (or above) is the way to go. These 3nm chipsets pack the best GPUs, which enable huge graphical capabilities such as hardware-accelerated ray tracing. Plus, this additional power means you can breeze through graphically intense productivity tasks, too.
 Size and weight: If portability is important to you, the MacBook Airs are a must-buy from this selection. From a weight of just 2.7 pounds for the 13-inch version (and a mere 3.3 pounds for the 15-inch), these are so easy to carry around. If portability isn't the biggest concern, you could go all the way up to 4.3 pounds for the 16-inch MacBook Pro . But as far as dimensions go, all of these models are seriously sleek and carryable.
 Battery life: The 16-inch M5 Pro MacBook Pro is the longest-lasting MacBook there is, posting a Tom's Guide battery test time of 21 hours and 10 minutes. But the whole MacBook lineup lasts 13 hours and above, so if longevity is your primary concern, each model will have you covered for a full workday.
 How we test every MacBook 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Outside of putting them through their real-life paces in our day-to-day, we have an advanced suite of lab tests to truly see what performance and power efficiency are like in every single MacBook. Go behind the scenes and check out all the lab tests we do !
 To get straight to the point of the key reasons people buy a MacBook — speed and battery life — we use our Geekbench 6 performance testing and the speed of transcoding video (Handbrake) to find out how well each MacBook performs, along with battery test to see how long these machines last before needing a charge.
 Beyond these, we test the display with a high-end colorimeter and brightness tester — to ensure you're getting a great panel for the price. Then, we move on to professional performance and graphics-intensive tasks like Pugetbench benchmarks with Adobe apps.
 And finally, as Apple is now really going hard on MacBook gaming, we have plenty of game benchmarks, including Cyberpunk 2077 !

 How many displays can be connected to MacBook Air
 The number of external displays that you can use at the same time depends on your Mac model and the resolution and refresh rate of each display.

 Best premium attached or stacked option: Mobile Pixels Duex Float 2 Pro

 The 2.9-pound listed weight is the decisive trade-off. Nearly three pounds attached to or carried with a laptop can change the hinge balance, increase travel bulk, and require more power than a basic 60 Hz FHD panel. Verify the laptop’s physical fit, hinge strength, video output, and ability to drive 2560×1600 at 120 Hz before purchase.

 Best conventional one-cable monitor: Lenovo ThinkVision M14
 The ThinkVision M14 is the simplest conventional portable-monitor recommendation when the laptop has a full-function USB-C port with video output. Lenovo’s datasheet says the M14 can extend or duplicate a notebook display through one USB-C connection when the notebook provides the required video-capable USB-C port; the ThinkVision M14 datasheet documents that requirement.
 The M14 is not a lid-mounted extender in the same sense as the Duex products. The separate form factor avoids putting monitor weight on the laptop hinge and lets the user place the screen beside, above, or in portrait orientation. The compromise is extra desk space and a separate item to carry.
 Best fit: Hot-desking, travel, school, and office work where one native USB-C cable is more useful than an attached design.
 Best higher-resolution conventional monitor: Lenovo ThinkVision M14d
 The ThinkVision M14d is a good conventional portable-monitor choice for buyers who want more resolution than a basic FHD mobile display. Lenovo’s US buying page listed the M14d as a 14-inch IPS WXGA+ 60 Hz USB-C monitor at $327 when crawled. Price, exact regional model, and stock should be verified on the current Lenovo listing .
 The M14d is preferable to an attached extender when the user wants a monitor that can also serve with a desktop, dock, or another laptop. The product does not remove the need to check USB-C DisplayPort Alt Mode and power delivery.
 Best touchscreen: ASUS ZenScreen Touch MB16AMTR

 OLED’s contrast and color advantages may be unnecessary for ordinary office work, where a less expensive IPS display can be sufficient. It can suit buyers who like the Float concept but do not need the Duex Float 2 Pro’s higher resolution and refresh rate. The Lenovo mobile USB monitor listing should be checked for the exact current model name, weight, brightness, refresh rate, ports, and availability.
 This product deserves a cautious recommendation because the available listing does not establish every specification needed for a confident comparison. Verify the return policy and test the physical stacking arrangement immediately.
 How do you check laptop compatibility before buying? 
 The most important compatibility check is not whether a laptop has a USB-C-shaped connector. The relevant USB-C port must support DisplayPort Alt Mode, Thunderbolt, or USB4 display output, or the setup must use HDMI/Mini HDMI or DisplayLink.
 Find the exact laptop model number. Do not rely on the series name alone; ports and display limits can differ within one family.
 Check the USB-C port specification. Look for “DisplayPort Alt Mode,” “Thunderbolt,” “USB4,” or a display icon in the laptop documentation. Charging-only USB-C cannot drive a native USB-C monitor.
 Check power output. Video capability and power capability are separate. A port may carry video but fail to supply enough power for a bright or large screen.
 Check HDMI or Mini HDMI options. HDMI may carry video while USB supplies power, if the extender or monitor supports that arrangement.
 Check the maximum number of displays. Confirm the laptop manufacturer’s GPU, dock, operating-system, and processor limits. A triple-screen accessory cannot bypass every hardware limit.
 Check the operating system and drivers. Native USB-C video is usually simpler. DisplayLink and hybrid-signal modes may need drivers, permissions, or IT approval.
 Check physical fit. Measure the laptop lid and examine the hinge, ports, webcam, vents, and mounting surface before ordering an attached product.
 Lenovo’s M14 documentation is especially clear that one-cable operation depends on a notebook with a full-function USB-C port supporting video. Mobile Pixels lists USB-C and Mini HDMI paths across its Duex products, but the laptop still must provide compatible video and sufficient power. Manufacturer-stated compatibility is a starting point, not a guarantee for every laptop configuration.
 Will one USB-C cable power and drive the extra display? 
 One USB-C cable can carry video and power together, but the result depends on the laptop port, cable, monitor, resolution, brightness, and refresh rate. Video, USB data, laptop charging, and monitor power pass-through are separate functions.

Test the setup while the laptop charger is connected.
 How do MacBooks, Chromebooks, Linux laptops, and Windows PCs differ? 
 MacBook compatibility cannot be reduced to “yes” or “no.” The result depends on the Mac’s Intel or Apple silicon generation, macOS version, native Thunderbolt or USB-C display support, number of supported external displays, and whether DisplayLink is involved.
 Mobile Pixels lists Windows, macOS, ChromeOS, and Linux compatibility for the Duex Float 2 Pro, Duex Max DS, and Duex Plus DS. Treat those statements as manufacturer claims and verify the exact model, connection method, and operating-system version before purchase.
 Native USB-C DisplayPort monitors are generally simpler on Windows, macOS, ChromeOS, and Linux than driver-dependent alternatives. Linux support can depend on the distribution and driver version. ChromeOS may support external screens while omitting proprietary rotation, touch, or control features. Wireless casting usually supports fewer combinations than wired video.
 DisplayLink can add a display when native outputs are insufficient, but DisplayLink is not equivalent to native DisplayPort Alt Mode. DisplayLink may require drivers, screen-recording or accessibility permissions on macOS, corporate IT approval, periodic updates, and acceptance of possible compression, latency, CPU usage, or playback restrictions.
 How many monitors can a laptop actually run? 
 The laptop’s maximum number of independent displays—not the number of panels in the accessory—determines the usable result. A triple-screen kit may show one working display, duplicate screens, or detect a panel without enabling it when the laptop, operating system, USB-C connection, GPU, or dock cannot support the requested configuration.
 Check the laptop manufacturer’s documentation for supported internal-plus-external and external-only display counts. If one panel works and another remains blank, test a different Thunderbolt, USB-C, or HDMI port, verify the laptop charger is connected, and confirm whether the accessory needs DisplayLink. A compatible multi-monitor dock can help in some cases; DisplayLink is an option only when its driver and performance trade-offs are acceptable.
 Is a clip-on extender safe for a laptop lid? 
 No attached extender should be described as universally safe for every laptop. The added weight, center of gravity, mounting system, lid material, hinge strength, and required viewing angle all affect the result.
 Measure the lid and compare it with the manufacturer’s laptop-size guidance.
 Consider whether the lid is metal, plastic, unusually thin, or already loose.
 Inspect magnetic or adhesive mounting before committing to a permanent setup.
 Check whether the display blocks a webcam, hinge, vent, side port, or power button.
 Check whether the laptop must remain open at a particular angle for stability.
 Do not carry an open laptop by the lid with a heavy extender attached.
 Use a separate monitor if hinge stress, portability, or desk ergonomics is a concern.
 Side-mounted screens can create a very wide setup that encourages neck rotation. Stacked screens can place the webcam at an awkward angle or force the user to look too high. A separate monitor on a stable stand may be ergonomically better even when the attached design packs more neatly for travel.
 Independent reader support Your contribution helps us test, update, and keep practical guides available for everyone. Support on Ko-Fi Which screen specifications matter for productivity? 
 Resolution, aspect ratio, brightness, weight, power requirements, and stand quality matter more for most office users than headline screen count.
 Resolution: FHD is adequate for many portable work displays; higher resolutions make text sharper but can cost more and use more power.
 Aspect ratio: 16:10 adds vertical workspace for documents, code, spreadsheets, and web pages. 16:9 can match common laptop panels and suit video or gaming.
 Brightness: Compare the manufacturer’s brightness specification with the laptop’s panel. A dimmer second screen can be tiring to use beside a bright laptop.
 Refresh rate: 60 Hz is generally adequate for office work. Higher refresh rates can make scrolling and games feel smoother while increasing cost and potentially power use.
 Color: OLED, wide-gamut, and HDR features matter for media and color-sensitive work, but are unnecessary for ordinary email and documents.
 Weight and thickness: These affect both travel comfort and the mechanical load of an attached product.
 Stand and port placement: A stable stand, useful viewing angle, portrait support, and cable access can matter more than a small specification advantage.
 Touch and battery: Both add flexibility but also cost and weight.
 For example, the Duex Float 2 Pro’s listed 2560×1600, 350-nit, 120 Hz specification is substantially more ambitious than the Duex Max DS and Duex Plus DS’s listed 1920×1080, 300-nit, 60 Hz class. ViewSonic’s VG1656N instead prioritizes a 16:10 1920×1200 workspace, battery, and wireless features.
 Is 16:10 better than 16:9 for work? 
 16:10 is usually better for documents, code, spreadsheets, and web pages because the taller panel provides more vertical workspace, while 16:9 can be preferable for video, gaming, and matching common laptop displays.
 An aspect-ratio mismatch is not normally a compatibility problem. The laptop and extender can use different ratios, although the setup may look less uniform and windows may need manual resizing.

 Is touchscreen support worth paying for? 
 Touch is worth paying for when the workflow includes presentations, signatures, creative tools, tablet-style interaction, or field use; touch usually adds little value to ordinary email and browser multitasking.
 Touch can also add glare, weight, cost, and operating-system limitations. Confirm that touch works over the selected connection and with the intended operating system rather than assuming that a USB-C video connection automatically carries touch input.

 Choose an attached product only when the integrated form factor solves a real problem. Choose a separate portable monitor when flexibility, lower hinge risk, independent placement, or use with multiple devices matters more than packing everything into one laptop-shaped unit.
 How should you set up a laptop screen extender? 
 Native USB-C setup
 Connect a full-featured USB-C video cable to the laptop’s DisplayPort Alt Mode, Thunderbolt, or USB4 port.
 Connect the other end to the monitor’s USB-C video port.
 Connect external power if the monitor flickers, refuses to start, runs dimly, or drains the laptop rapidly.
 Open the operating system’s display settings and choose Extend rather than Duplicate or Mirror.
 Drag the virtual displays into their physical left-to-right or top-to-bottom arrangement.
 Set the recommended resolution and refresh rate, then test sleep, wake, rotation, and webcam use.
 HDMI plus USB-power setup
 Connect the laptop’s HDMI output to the monitor’s HDMI or Mini HDMI input with the correct cable or adapter.
 Connect the monitor’s USB power cable to the laptop, charger, or power bank.
 Select the correct input on the monitor.
 Configure Extend in the operating system’s display settings.
 DisplayLink setup
 Install the current DisplayLink software from the hardware maker or DisplayLink source appropriate to the operating system.
 Approve required macOS screen-recording or accessibility permissions and any corporate security prompts.
 Connect the DisplayLink adapter, dock, or monitor.
 Test ordinary windows first, then video playback and demanding applications.
 Expect possible latency, compression, CPU/GPU overhead, driver updates, or protected-content restrictions.
 Windows, macOS, and ChromeOS checks
 On Windows, use Settings > System > Display to select Extend these displays and arrange the screens. On macOS, open System Settings > Displays, select the display arrangement, and choose whether the screens extend or mirror. ChromeOS display controls are available through Settings > Device > Displays, although proprietary rotation, touch, and control features may not be supported.
 What should you do when the extra screen is blank or flickers? 
 Confirm that the monitor is powered and set to the correct input.
 Replace the USB-C cable with a full-featured video-capable cable.
 Move the cable to a USB-C, Thunderbolt, or USB4 port documented as supporting display output.
 Connect the laptop’s charger and, if available, the monitor’s external power adapter.
 Lower brightness, resolution, or refresh rate to reduce the power and bandwidth demand.
 Test HDMI video with separate USB power if the monitor supports HDMI.
 Check whether the laptop supports the requested number of independent displays.
 Install or update DisplayLink or hybrid-signal software only when the product requires it.
 Restart the laptop after installing a display driver or changing macOS permissions.
 Test the product on the intended laptop before the return window closes.

 Buy the Mobile Pixels Duex Max DS for an attached second screen on a larger laptop, or the Duex Plus DS for a smaller laptop. Choose the Duex Float 2 Pro when high resolution and 120 Hz matter more than weight. Choose the Trio 3.0 Pro only after confirming that the laptop can drive two additional independent displays.
 For most buyers, a separate native USB-C portable monitor is the lower-risk choice. The Lenovo ThinkVision M14 family, Lenovo M15, Lenovo L15, ViewSonic VG1656-2K, or Mobile Pixels Glance 16 can be repositioned without loading the laptop hinge. Choose ASUS MB16AMTR for touch, ASUS MQ16AHE for OLED color and contrast, and ViewSonic VG1656N for wireless or battery-powered presentations.
 Before placing an order, verify the exact laptop model, USB-C video support, cable requirements, external-display limit, power needs, operating-system behavior, physical fit, warranty, and return policy. Test every display mode immediately after delivery.
 Frequently Asked Questions 
 Does every USB-C laptop support a portable monitor?
 No. The laptop’s USB-C port must support DisplayPort Alt Mode, Thunderbolt, or USB4 display output for native USB-C video. A charging-only or data-only USB-C port cannot drive a native USB-C monitor without another video method such as HDMI or DisplayLink.
 Can a laptop run a triple-screen extender?
 A laptop can run a triple-screen extender only when the laptop, operating system, GPU, connection method, and accessory together support the required number of independent displays. The number of panels in the kit does not override the laptop’s display-output limit.
 Are attached laptop screen extenders safe for every laptop?
 No attached extender is proven safe for every laptop. Buyers must consider the extender’s weight, center of gravity, mounting method, lid material, hinge strength, webcam, vents, ports, and required lid angle. A separate portable monitor avoids adding weight to the laptop hinge.
 Is DisplayLink as good as native USB-C video?
 DisplayLink is useful when a laptop lacks enough native video outputs, but DisplayLink is not equivalent to native DisplayPort Alt Mode. DisplayLink may require drivers and permissions and can introduce compression, latency, CPU usage, driver maintenance, or protected-content limitations.
 Is 16:10 better than 16:9 on a laptop screen extender?
 16:10 is usually better for documents, coding, spreadsheets, and web pages because it provides more vertical workspace. 16:9 can be preferable for video, gaming, or matching a common laptop display, and the two aspect ratios can work together without creating a basic compatibility problem.
 The Bottom Line 
 Bottom line: Choose an attached Duex model only when integrated placement is worth the added weight and hinge load. For the broadest compatibility and lowest mechanical risk, buy a separate native USB-C portable monitor after confirming DisplayPort Alt Mode, power, display-count, and operating-system support.

 When folded up, the Trio 3 Pro measures 13.4 x 8.8 x 0.9 inches (34 x 22.4 x 2.3cm). In all its unfurled glory, it spans 40.3 inches (just over 1m) but can be pulled closer together if your available desk space doesn’t stretch that far.
 It’s a design that will either excite you with its screen breadth or scare you with its wingspan. It looks cumbersome but is actually quite light and flexible. The Trio 3 Pro’s protective and subtly magnetic folio cover doubles up as an integrated stand that is reasonably firm.

The price is high but this portable all-environment, 2-in-1 screen might solve your display needs away from a standard desk setup.

 Best overall premium attached system: Xebec Snap. Best for maximum attached screen area: Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro . Best flexible alternative: a standalone 15.6-inch-class USB-C portable monitor such as Plugable’s portable display. Best for a vertical workspace: Mobile Pixels Duex Float . The right choice depends less on the number of panels than on USB-C video support, mounting stability, power, and whether you truly need the display attached to the laptop.
 Buying note: This guide is framed around 2025 buying decisions. Prices, stock, warranties, included cables, operating-system support, and retailer listings can change, so verify those details immediately before ordering. The recommendations below are based on manufacturer specifications and independent buying-guide and review evidence, not hands-on testing.
 Quick verdict 
 A laptop screen extender is worth buying when you want additional displays that travel with the computer. For a polished premium setup, choose Xebec Snap . For the largest attached workspace, choose Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro . If you want to place the second display independently, avoid loading the laptop lid, or connect it to several kinds of devices, a standalone portable monitor for laptops is usually the more flexible choice. For a narrow desk or vertical workflow, look at the Mobile Pixels Duex Float family.

 1. Xebec Snap: best premium attached system 
 Xebec Snap is the strongest choice for someone who wants an integrated, laptop-mounted workstation rather than a loose monitor beside the computer. Xebec says its universal Snap Bracket works with any laptop and does not use magnets, adhesives, or conventional clips. The Snap system is built around that bracket, with official configurations that provide either a dual-screen or tri-screen arrangement.
 The screens are listed as 13.3-inch Full HD panels. They can be used in portrait or landscape orientation, and Xebec documents a 270-degree presentation rotation. Embedded USB-C cables and modular accessories, including options such as a light or phone charger, make the system more coherent than combining a generic monitor with a collection of unrelated mounts.
 Why it stands out: the bracket, cables, rotation options, and accessories are designed as one system. That makes it appealing for professionals who frequently move between a desk, meeting room, and home office and want the displays to travel with the laptop.
 Important limitation: the Snap Screen requires the Snap Bracket. Xebec’s support material does not position it as a generic monitor that can be attached to arbitrary stands or used with any spare cable. Pass-through charging is also documented as part of the bracket system, so confirm the exact configuration and power path before buying.
 Choose Xebec Snap if: you value a polished mounting system, need portrait and presentation modes, and are willing to pay for an integrated ecosystem.
 Think twice if: your laptop lid is unusually thin or flexible, you frequently work on a lap or airplane tray, or you want a display that can be detached and used independently with other devices.
